newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugul Tapado power plant on stream in early '98.
newsitem.headline: Portugul Tapado power plant on stream in early '98.

text.p: The Tapada power plant in northern Portugal, described as the most advanced being built in Europe, will supply 20 percent of Portugal's electricity and may export energy to Spain after commercial operations start in March 1998, its general manager said.

The 1,000 MW plant will use natural gas sent down a $1.88 billion pipeline from Algeria via Morocco and Spain to Portugal, said Graham Miles, general manager and director of joint venture company Turbogas, owner of the plant.
He said the first natural gas supplies were expected to reach Portugal next month and to reach the plant at Tapada do Outeiro, 18 km (11 miles) southeast of Oporto, in October 1997.
The plant will have three units, each with 330 MW capacity. The first unit is expected to come on stream by March 1998, the second by September 1998 and the third by May 1999.
"The first unit is on time. The second and third units could be ready ahead of schedule," Miles told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday. Portugal needs some 5000 MW capacity in the winter.
The Tapada plant, which employs 45 people, will turn 55 percent of the natural gas it receives into electricity, a much higher rate of efficiency than a coal-fired power plant.
The plant combines the latest gas and steam turbine technology, Miles said. "It is the most advanced power plant being built in Europe," he said.
Turbogas's main shareholder is British generator PowerGen, operator of the plant, which holds a 50 percent stake minus one share.
The other shareholders are Portuguese state-owned electricity compony EDP-Electricidade de Portugal and German companies RWE, Siemens and Koch.
Siemens and Koch are building the plant under a turnkey construction contract awarded to them by Turbogas.

Turbogas has a power purchase agreement with its client the Portuguese national grid, Rede Electrica Nacional (REN), a unit of EDP, and a gas supply agreement with state company Transgas, which will supply the Algerian natural gas to Tapada.
PowerGen will receive income from REN for providing the capacity and energy and will pay Transgas for receiving the gas.
When the power purchase (PPA) and gas supply agreements run out 25 years after the start of commercial operations, ownership of Tapada will transfer to REN unless the PPA is renewed.
Miles said Tapada, the biggest combined cycle power plant in Iberia, would be capable of exporting electricity to Spain.
The two countries already export electricity to each other under a bilateral agreement.
"It will be REN's choice whether to export or not," Miles said. "REN could export to Spain."
However, in the absence of a liberalised energy market across the European Union, it was unlikely to export elsewhere.

Asked what had been done to guarantee electricity production if civil strife in Algeria were to halt natural gas supplies, Miles said he believed disruptions were unlikely as all parties in Algeria accepted that the pipeline provided vital revenue.
However, he said that Turbogas had a contract with state oil company Petrogal to supply distillate, or diesel fuel, to Tapada, which would carry a five-day stock.
"We have the ability to burn gasoil (diesel)," he said.
